originality.rationale: Gill (2024) proves the binary length-four two-state cases and negative 0100; Kjos-Hanssen (2026) gives three states on every alphabet. Neither establishes that every length-four word with three or four distinct letters has a two-state witness. Seven multiletter patterns, the arbitrary-alphabet extension and the exact q(q-1) classification fill that gap, with residual priority risk.
residual_risks: The full final sections of arXiv:2607.26275 were inaccessible for inspection; its abstract and introduction explicitly distinguish the all-alphabet three-state bound from the complete binary classification.
Unindexed or terminology-divergent work could have independently derived the thirteen small witness cases; no independent priority review performed.

value.rationale: Complete first nontrivial short-word classification across every finite alphabet size, where 0100 is the first binary word requiring three states. The exact q(q-1) count, identification of the unique exceptional equality pattern, and explicit two-state witness for four pairwise distinct symbols are nontrivial information about state-minimal probabilistic recognition not entailed by existing binary-only or three-state bounds.
